Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

commitment noun

dedication to a task, a cause or a person

also dedication, be committed to, committed, dedicated, devoted

classical

Cic. Inv. 1.36: studium est animī assidua et vehemēns ad aliquam rem applicāta magnā cum voluntāte occupātiō (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Sen. 22: modo permaneat studium et industria

studium, studiī n.

noun, second declension; <span lang="la">studium alicujus reī</span>, commitment to something

zeal, eager and steady application, commitment

Cicero’s definition is the English word: the mind’s steady, vigorous application to something, with a will. It is also goodwill towards a person, and very often a pursuit or a study (studia, one’s studies). For a promise one has made, see promise.

Other words

  • dēditus, dēdita, dēditum — committed, devoted (to)

    participle of dēdō as an adjective, with the dative · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 12.16.1: dēditum optimīs studiīs

    Lewis & Short: “given up to, addicted, devoted to something; eager, assiduous”, especially frequent in Cicero, and used of bad things as of good. The verb dēdō is to give up, surrender.

Examples

  • manent ingenia senibus, modo permaneat studium et industria

    the old keep their wits, provided their commitment and hard work lastCic. Sen. 22

  • vīdī fīlium tuum dēditum optimīs studiīs summāque modestiae fāmā

    I saw your son committed to the best studies and with the highest reputation for good conductCic. Fam. 12.16.1

  • nē exspectēmus quidem, dum rogēmur; studium semper adsit, cūnctātiō absit

    let us not even wait to be asked; let there always be eagerness and never hesitationCic. Amic. 44

See also effort, promise, commitment.

SourcesLewis & Short: studium · Lewis & Short: deditus
